reason: Multiple independent sources document JPL's origin as the Caltech 'Suicide Squad' and its subsequent evolution into NASA's planetary exploration center.
story: In 1936, rocket science was considered reckless science fiction. At Caltech, graduate student Frank Malina teamed up with self-taught rocket enthusiasts Jack Parsons and Edward Forman to test dangerous homemade rocket motors. After a series of hazardous tests and explosions—including one that blasted an instrument gauge straight into a laboratory wall—the group was dubbed the 'Suicide Squad' and ordered off campus. Banished to the Arroyo Seco, a dry riverbed wash in Pasadena, the team continued their work using alcohol-fueled engines. Their successful experiments on Jet-Assisted Take-Off rockets soon attracted U.S. Army funding. By 1943, team members proposed naming their venture the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. After building Explorer 1, America's first satellite, in 1958, JPL was transferred to NASA. The ragtag band of campus outcasts ultimately laid the foundation for the agency that sent rovers across Mars and propelled Voyager into interstellar space.
angle: NASA's premier planetary exploration center, JPL, was founded by a ragtag crew of amateur rocketeers nicknamed the 'Suicide Squad' after getting kicked off Caltech's campus for blowing up a lab.

claims.claim: JPL traces its beginnings to rocket experiments that started in the Arroyo Seco riverbed wash on Halloween in 1936.
Caltech graduate student Frank Malina led the early rocket propulsion experiments.
Caltech aeronautics professor Theodore von Kármán served as Frank Malina's advisor and oversaw the rocketry research.
Self-taught rocket experimenters Jack Parsons and Edward Forman teamed up with Malina to build rocket motor designs.
The rocketeers were dubbed the 'Suicide Squad' by people on the Caltech campus due to hazardous tests and explosions.
After hazardous test explosions on campus, the squad was forced to move operations away from Caltech to the Arroyo Seco.
The team's initial outdoor tests in 1936 evaluated small, alcohol-fueled rocket motors.
Caltech student Qian Xuesen was an early member of the rocketry group and co-authored the proposal using the name Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
The rocketry group developed Jet-Assisted Take-Off (JATO) rockets to help propeller aircraft take off from short runways.
The Caltech rocketry group first adopted the name 'Jet Propulsion Laboratory' in a 1943 research proposal.
JPL and the Army Ballistic Missile Agency built and launched America's first satellite, Explorer 1, on January 31, 1958.
In December 1958, JPL was officially transferred from U.S. Army control to the newly created NASA.
JPL built and operates NASA's Deep Space Network antenna complexes located at Goldstone, near Madrid, and near Canberra.
NASA launched the twin Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft under JPL management in 1977.
Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, becoming the first human-made craft to do so.
Voyager 2 became the only spacecraft to conduct flybys of all four giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
JPL mission control staff observe a tradition of eating 'lucky peanuts' before risky maneuvers and critical mission events.
The lucky peanuts tradition originated on the Ranger 7 lunar mission after six consecutive Ranger mission failures.
JPL operates as a federally funded research and development center managed by the California Institute of Technology.
In January 2025, JPL's facility was closed and evacuated as the nearby Eaton Fire threatened the area.

disputed: Identity of the person who introduced lucky peanuts: S4 credits trajectory engineer Dick Wallace, while S1 notes it may have been either Wallace or project manager Harris Schurmeier. The script should attribute the act to 'a team member' or state 'according to one account, trajectory engineer Dick Wallace passed them out'.
Campus size: S1 and S3 report JPL covers approximately 168 acres, whereas S4 reports a 177-acre site. The script should avoid citing an exact acreage figure.
